figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Challenges in Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution. The camera first observes a subject (a vendor and his handcart), moves away to reveal a newly requested event (a collapsing building facade), and then moves back to the original scene. Previous methods (rows 1–4) exhibit various failures. In contrast, EvoWorld (row 5) realizes the event, revisits the original subject, and renders a causally plausible reaction while preserving subject and scene consistency.
figures.headline: Four prior models show missing reactions, duplicated subjects or drift, while EvoWorld realizes the event and reveals a plausible reaction.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 1, HY-World 1.5 (HunyuanWorld, 2025), Echo-WM (Zhang et al., 2026b), LingBot-World (Team et al., 2026b), and SANA-WM (Zhu et al., 2026) exhibit various failures: the event or reaction may be absent, the subject may follow the camera or become duplicated, appearance and background may drift, or the subject may exhibit implausible behavior.

Specifically, as shown in Fig. 1, an Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution rollout can be abstracted into at least three semantic parts (each corresponding to at least one prompt): (1) $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{init}}$ (initial): the part that covers the initial state of the scenario and the main subjects.

figures.caption: Overview of the data engine for EvoWorld. Structured scenarios are rendered into single-take out-of-sight interactions, verified against visual evidence, temporally annotated, and converted into a training supervision dataset and evaluation benchmark.
figures.headline: The data engine turns structured scenarios into verified, temporally annotated single-take videos used for both training and benchmarking.
citing_sentences: Fig. 2 shows the overall data construction pipeline of EvoWorld.

figures.caption: Examples and statistics of EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench. The upper part illustrates representative training and benchmark examples, while the lower part summarizes their scale and scenario diversity.
figures.headline: Examples and statistics show EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench cover 50+ fine-grained scene and sub-event types.
citing_sentences: After semantic deduplication, the benchmark covers 50+ fine-grained scene types and sub-event types, as summarized in Fig. 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Overview of the EvoWorld framework. (a) Stage 1 learns out-of-sight reactive rendering. (b) Stage 2 refines the renderer through online autoregressive adaptation. (c) Inference uses brain–renderer collaboration for Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution.
figures.headline: The framework runs in three parts: reactive rendering training, online autoregressive adaptation, and brain-renderer inference for out-of-sight evolution.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Effect of event-conditioned reasoning prompts on Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution.
figures.headline: Replacing the brain's event-conditioned reasoning prompt with a blind revisit prompt lowers performance substantially, yet the variant stays above the baselines.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 5, performance drops substantially without event-conditioned reasoning, confirming its importance for inferring an appropriate response from the realized event.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison under the same VLM-brain reasoning prompt.
figures.headline: Under the same reasoning prompt, baselines show hallucinated events, subject duplication or coarse revisits, while EvoWorld keeps the subject and scene.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 6, the baselines exhibit hallucinated event entities, subject duplication, or coarse revisit frames, whereas EvoWorld preserves the subject and scene while rendering a coherent defensive response.

For a more detailed ablation, the prompt-transfer and shared-prompt analyses in Tables 3 and 6 also provide baseline renderers with the brain-generated reasoning prompt, allowing us to separate the contribution of event-conditioned reasoning from that of the proposed data and renderer training.

abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain–renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

sections.body: The introduction argues that video world models mostly preserve or retrieve earlier visual states, but lack an explicit way to reason about how events change entities. It defines Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution: render an event, infer its consequences for a subject that is out of view, and show the result when the camera returns. Figure 1 shows HY-World 1.5, Echo-WM, LingBot-World and SANA-WM with failures such as absent reactions, duplicated subjects and appearance drift. The paper contributes the problem formulation, the EvoWorld brain-renderer framework, EvoWorld-Data with around 12k videos, and EvoWorld-Bench.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Out-of-sight causal evolution requires video models to reason about event consequences, not only preserve visual history.

sections.body: The related work reviews video world models and segment-autoregressive generators such as LingBot-World-v2, Echo-WM, YUME-1.5, Matrix-Game 3.0 and BiWM. It states that long-horizon consistency does not guarantee that an unobserved world continues to change. Prior out-of-sight work, including ReMind, LiveWorld and Hybrid Memory, mainly tests whether a motion continues through an observation gap. The paper's setting differs by introducing an event after the subject leaves view and inferring its consequences when the subject returns.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing long-horizon video models preserve consistency, but do not ensure unobserved worlds keep evolving.

sections.body: The section defines three parts of a rollout: an initial state, an event after the subject leaves the frame, and a revisit that must show a causally plausible reaction. EvoWorld-Data contains around 12k videos of at least ten seconds, generated from scripts and checked for camera return and subject reappearance. EvoWorld-Bench has 120 cases, with 69 photorealistic and 51 game/virtual. The renderer uses an entity anchor for subject identity and the four preceding latents as a temporal anchor. Identity-Anchored Attention strengthens attention to the entity anchor on revisit windows. Training has two stages: reactive rendering from clean ground-truth windows, then online autoregressive rollout training from self-generated predecessors.
sections.heading: EvoWorld: Data and Method
sections.headline: EvoWorld pairs a vision-language model brain with a video renderer, trained on a 12k-video dataset in two stages.

sections.body: EvoWorld is compared with LingBot-World, LingBot-World-v2, YUME-1.5, SANA-WM, Echo-WM and the Evoke variants on EvoWorld-Bench. Core Task Success requires event success, revisit success and full causal plausibility in the same case. Evoke-Turbo reaches 98.3% Revisit Success and 89.2% Event Success, but the paper reports that its Core Task Success and Causal Plausibility show successful components do not form a coherent event-reaction chain. The authors report that EvoWorld keeps high subject consistency, background consistency, visual integrity and motion smoothness. Scores come mainly from a Qwen3.8 judge, with VBench motion smoothness as a secondary diagnostic.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: EvoWorld reaches 90.8% Core Task Success, exceeding the second-best baseline by 69.1 percentage points.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the problem formulation and the construction of EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench. It summarizes the framework as a reasoning-augmented brain-renderer collaboration trained with identity-anchored attention and a two-stage procedure. It states that experiments show substantial gains over recent video world models while preserving generation quality and consistency. It points to the appendix for limitations and future directions.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Conclusion: EvoWorld improves out-of-sight causal evolution over recent video world models while keeping quality and consistency.

sections.body: The appendix describes EvoWorld-Data construction from structured tuples, script generation and verification of camera return and subject reappearance. EvoWorld-Bench is screened against training data visually and semantically. Event and revisit success are binary, while causal plausibility, reaction quality and consistency use a three-level scale. Core success requires revisit, event and causal plausibility of 1 together. The appendix also gives training hyperparameters, one-shot baselines, and MiniMax-H3 with 21.7% Core Task Success. Stated limitations are the single-event, single-reaction scope and mostly horizontal camera trajectories.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers data construction, benchmark screening, metric definitions, training settings, one-shot baselines, MiniMax-H3 results and limitations.
